name: Nanticoke
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Extinct; only 18th-c. vocabularies (Murray 1792, Heckewelder) attested, no grammar or stress description

sources.citation: Speck, Frank G. 1915. The Nanticoke Community of Delaware. Contributions from the Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation 2(4)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ethnography of the Delaware community; no Nanticoke-language data beyond citing Murray/Brinton; the phrase 'with a rising accent' (p. 42-43) refers to an English greeting, not Nanticoke.

Tertiary. Phonology section (consonants, vowels, /l/~[r] word-finally) cites Cunningham 2023/2024 dissertation and gives its direct PDF URL; repeats Murray's '!' = 'peculiar, forcible, explosive, enunciation' of a syllable; no statement on word stress placement.

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1893. A Vocabulary of the Nanticoke Dialect. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 31(142): 325-333 (prints William Vans Murray's 1792 vocabulary with Murray's covering letter to Jefferson)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress rule. The only prosodic remark is Brinton's note on p. 327: 'The exclamation point, !, so frequently introduced by Mr. Murray, he explains to signify a peculiar, forcible, explosive enunciation of the syllable.' (e.g. 'Bread, app!ow', 'Belly, nut-ah !', 'Chesnut-tree, eh !qua-mintz'). The '!' is not analysed as stress by Brinton.

sources.citation: Cunningham, Keith Andrew. 2023. A Phonological Analysis of Nanticoke With Practical Applications for Language Revitalization. PhD dissertation, Georgetown University, 425 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: open copy online (also online with a university library login)
sources.note: The only descriptive source Glottolog lists (listed by Glottolog as a phonology) and the only modern phonological analysis of the language; a 425-page phonology built from the Murray and Heckewelder vocabularies is the one place a Nanticoke stress statement (or a statement that stress is unrecoverable) would be made. Wikipedia's phonology section is drawn from it.

sources.citation: Cunningham, Keith; Hall, Karelle; Rain, Ragghi. 2023. Once It Has Been Spoken.. It Cannot Be Unspoken. Salt Water Media. ISBN 978-1628063714.
